Konica/Minolta have recently filed an interesting patent application, United States Patent Application 20040142248:

It refers to a silver halide emulsion that requires no wet development. It is developed simply by heat.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: Unfortunately it's going to take an hour or so to really get into the patent. However, on briefly reading it through, it seems to be a variation of the Polaroid method, but with different materials and a different mechanism. From a first glance (probably wrong, it's pretty obfuscating!) it seems that his Silver Halide contains other materials which promote the reduction of Silver, I think that's what the metals and gold sensitization is for. The "processing material" he talks of is then attached to the Silver halide and this combined system is heated. Whatever is in the processing layer then processes the Silver halide. The whole point being that it's no longer wet processed in trays. You simply zap the shot, stick this "processing material" to the Silver and heat. The various solutions etc in the material go into the Silver and you almost get self-developing. As I said, it's reminescent of the old Polaroid cameras - if I'm right.

posts.content_md:
> **MichaelH:** Is it simply heat? Perhaps I found the wrong patent but this onePatent linkseems to use a lot of wet baths for processing.Then again, when reading a patent application I tend to feel like I'm being spun in a circle by all the obfuscation.

The emulsion is based on "organic silver". This kind of emulsions has been known for quite a while. It's used mostly for lithographic applications.

Regarding the processing, it's only the development that is carried out by heat. Bleaching, fixing still require wet processing...

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Itb seems from this claim:

[i:2c91b2601c]wherein the hydrophilic colloid layer of the silver halide photographic material further contains an insoluble metal oxide or an insoluble metal hydroxide.[/i:2c91b2601c]

that is not just silver halide. Also, they seem to back the silver halide with a "processing memberl":

[i:2c91b2601c]superimposing the developed silver halide photographic material with a processing member in the presence of an aqueous solvent; and

[0022] (v) separating the processing member superimposed on a surface of the developed silver halide photographic material to obtain the holographic stereogram,[/i:2c91b2601c]

which seems to to do the actual developing, ie amplification of the specks.

There is a pretty detailed method of manufacture of the processing member. My guess would be that there's some sort of ionisation process going on involving the metal oxide and metal hydroxide in conjunction with whatever is in the processing member that reduces the silver halide. This clearly needs heat to make the reaction go. I'd be curious to know what the gamma of the development scheme is. How does this reaction differentiate grains with specks on them to grains without?

My guess would be that there's some sort of ionisation process going on involving the metal oxide and metal hydroxide in conjunction with whatever is in the processing member that reduces the silver halide. This clearly needs heat to make the reaction go. I'd be curious to know what the gamma of the development scheme is. How does this reaction differentiate grains with specks on them to grains without?

I understand those thermally developable systems are still based on the formation of a latent image which is greatly reinforced by (thermal) development. So far, business as usual. A novelty is to make that kind of emulsions for holography. 

One might suspect this new emulsion has been designed particularly for the Voxel system. I don't know how important an issue it is to have those x-ray based stereograms bleached...
